speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Members may wish to withdraw the questions filed for future Sittings if they have had their questions addressed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We had tightened restrictions to slow the growth in the number of cases and to further expand and stabilise our healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I have been meeting the clinical teams that run the ICUs, visiting them on site to go through operational details and speaking to their staff to understand the challenges that they face.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These discussions and the insights shared are vital in helping us plan ahead should infection rates climb and severe cases increase.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For isolation beds, it is now at 85%.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The proportion of COVID-19 cases requiring ICU care is at about 0.3% today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some are intubated and require a mechanical ventilator.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These patients stay for an average of 11 to 15 days in the ICU and some stay for up to a month in the ICU.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Besides COVID-19 cases, there are also non-COVID-19 patients with life-threatening medical conditions who require ICU care, adding to the sustained load that our hospitals have to bear.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our public hospitals currently operate about 163 adult ICU beds for these patients, with an average occupancy of close to 80%.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In comparison, in 2019, before COVID-19 struck, we had 298 adult ICU beds, and the average occupancy rate was 63%.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we have been reducing the non-COVID-19 ICU beds, in order to cope with more COVID-19 patients.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is one of the key trade-offs when we increase the number of COVID-19 ICU beds.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have had to increase the total number of ICU beds to 382 for both COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 patients over the past two months.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And the need to increase the capacity of our healthcare system is a heavy burden carried by the staff, our healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Already, our hospitals are feeling the manpower crunch.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Signs of fatigue can be seen amongst our healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It has been over 20 months of continuous daily battle against the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: A large proportion of our healthcare workers have not had the opportunity to take leave since 2020 and over 90% of them will not be able to clear their accumulated leave for 2021.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is clearly a much higher proportion compared to the past two years.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our healthcare workers have gone and continue to go way beyond the call of duty to care for their patients.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The hospitals are trying to minimise having staff work overtime.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For the month of September, our nurses worked for an average of 160 to 175 hours per month.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I received a WhatsApp message from a senior member of the clinical teams.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It says, "We are getting increasingly stretched, overworked and fatigued...

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are uncertain how long we can keep this up.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Morale is slipping." Another colleague sent me a WhatsApp message and it goes: "It feels like what started as a 2.4km run became a marathon and just as we are reaching the finishing line, we have to run a second marathon.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our people are exhausted physically, mentally, emotionally – whether they will admit it or not." I know this person as a professional colleague.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Their roles to look after ICU patients also extend to looking after their staff, managing their teams, making sure that people are in a position and have the ability to perform at their best.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, when people like them say words like these, "exhausted physically, mentally, emotionally – whether they will admit it or not", I take it very, very seriously.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is therefore not surprising to find resignation rates going up this year.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: About 1,500 healthcare workers have resigned in the first half of 2021 compared to about 2,000 annually pre-pandemic.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Foreign healthcare workers have also resigned in bigger numbers, especially when they are unable to travel to see their families back home.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Close to 500 foreign doctors and nurses, healthcare workers, have resigned in the first half of 2021, as compared to around 500 in the whole of 2020 and around 600 in 2019, about double the usual rate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These resignations were mostly tendered for personal reasons, for migration, or moving back to their home countries.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But it is also in such trying circumstances that we find stories of inspiration, stories of commitment to public service.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On a recent visit to a COVID-19 ICU, I met a nurse who had been redeployed from her usual job in the Orthopaedic Department into the COVID-19 ICU.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In the Orthopaedic Department, they look after bones, joints, muscles and she was now redeployed into a COVID-19 ICU.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: She had had a short training and orientation course, and then subsequently on-the-job training from her ICU colleagues.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: She is senior, she is a Nurse Clinician and an Advanced Practice Nurse, with many, many decades in public service.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And although it is a challenge to work in a new environment and with a new set of equipment, drugs and protocols, because of her excellent fundamentals and her experience and resolve, she demonstrated confidence and competence in delivering care that the ICU patients need.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On the day I visited, she was looking after her first ever obstetric patient.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: After many years, this is her first ever obstetric patient, a young lady who had to have her baby delivered prematurely because of COVID-19 and was now needing treatment in the COVID-19 ICU, not in a post-natal ward.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: An orthopaedic nurse, deployed to a COVID-19 ICU, now looking after an obstetric patient.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And there are many others like her, doctors, nurses, therapists, social workers – re-deployed to do what is urgently needed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And despite having to do difficult work in unfamiliar environments they have kept the clinical outcomes excellent, through hard work, professionalism, dedication and resilience.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They are carrying a burden of care that is sometimes unimaginable.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Having to hold a phone for a patient so that the family can say their last goodbyes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Holding their patient's hand, to keep them company, on behalf of the relatives.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They need all the support we can give them.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At MOH, we are redeploying manpower, to serve as healthcare or patient care assistants at our institutions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are reaching out to more volunteers to join the SG Healthcare Corps and support this important work.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are collaborating with private hospitals to ease some of the load on our healthcare workers in our public hospitals.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are stepping up the recruitment of healthcare workers from overseas.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our public healthcare institutions have also stepped up their outreach to staff to support them through measures that will safeguard their well-being, including counselling services, staff helplines and peer support programmes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Healthcare workers who are concerned about the way sick leave affects their performance appraisals can approach their union, MOM or MOH for assistance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have been repurposing existing hospital wards, such as single rooms and isolation rooms, into additional ICU beds.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have been augmenting ICU manpower by deploying previously trained ICU staff to help with patient care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Non-ICU staff have also been brought in, as I described earlier, and they work under the supervision of ICU-trained staff.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The shift pattern of nurses may have to be adjusted in order to cater to these needs and this has already started to happen in some hospitals.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At the same time, we are also asking the private hospitals to set aside ICU beds to assist in managing both COVID-19 patients and non-COVID-19 patients who are critically ill.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Increasing ICU beds takes time and it affects regular hospital operations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Converting non-COVID-19 ICU beds for use by COVID-19 patients who need intensive care has a limit, as it diverts resources from non-COVID-19 patients who also need care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The most important limit is the manpower required to staff ICU beds.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Patients in ICU need trained staff, who must be able to provide individualised care, including round-the-clock monitoring and continuous care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, any increase in ICU bed capacity must be supported by an increase in manpower, which has to be diverted away from non-COVID-19 ICU duties.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Any redeployed staff or new hires would also have to undergo training to operate the specialised equipment and medical devices in the ICU to care for their COVID-19 patients.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Logistically, we can keep stepping up our ICU beds.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have ventilators, we have equipment, consumables, all the things that are needed, but not enough people.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As a result, if we keep increasing our beds, we stretch and stretch our healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will come to the point that they will no longer be able to provide that continuous excellent care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our nurse-to-patient ratio will also be lower, which means each nurse will have to take care of more patients than they do today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In a normal ICU – peacetime, pre-COVID-19 – one nurse would look after one or two patients.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If she has to look after four, she will not have enough hands or time to provide the same level of care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There will come a point where even as the healthcare professionals are doing their very best, they are trying their hardest, more patients will die.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And this will affect both COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 patients.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As more healthcare resources are diverted to support COVID-19 services, our hospitals' ability to sustain regular non-COVID-19 services will be reduced.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, while we may have plans to step up to a certain number of ICU beds, the real situation on the ground, the operational considerations, are not straightforward.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do not want to go anywhere near to this theoretical limit.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If we do, the situation can easily get out of hand.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It will affect the unvaccinated disproportionately, but it will also affect all the rest of us.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: MOH has strategies to restrict the number of cases, not only to try to shield our healthcare workers and hospitals from the large surges, but also to protect all of us.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to need care for heart disease, diabetes and cancer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will have accidents and broken bones, and all of the patients, all of us, will need care, comfort and healing.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our ICU staff have been stretched to their limit in the last two weeks.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The booster doses have helped in reducing severe illnesses among vaccinated seniors, but the unvaccinated continues to be at risk.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That is why we continue to monitor the situation very closely, especially the number of unvaccinated seniors who get infected.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Every day, there are about 60 of them and six are likely to end up in the ICU.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We need to keep this group as small as possible to ensure everyone who needs care can receive it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Thankfully, because of our high vaccination coverage, almost all cases, about 99%, have had no or mild symptoms.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Each death is a tragedy and a loss felt by the family, the patient's loved ones and the care team.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Of these, 395 of them passed away in a hospital, eight at home and four in a care facility.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The number of deaths has increased in the past two months as the overall number of cases increased.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Seniors who are unvaccinated and have underlying medical conditions are at much greater risk of severe illness and death.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Almost all of the remaining 28% who were fully vaccinated, suffered from underlying medical conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, cancer and heart, lung, or kidney diseases.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Underlying conditions add risks, even if the conditions are well controlled before the patient encounters COVID-19, especially if the patient is elderly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is not yet conclusive information about the long-term health consequences of COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: An NCID study found that one in 10 COVID-19 patients who recovered after the initial infection continued to display symptoms such as coughing or breathlessness six months after recovering from the acute illness.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: A study in the UK found that those who are vaccinated are half as likely to continue having symptoms about a month after COVID-19 infection as compared to those who are unvaccinated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: While most of our cases recover fully from COVID-19, we do see instances of re-infection.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Up to mid-August, we had detected 32 re-infected cases and all of them were unvaccinated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So far, we have had one of the lowest fatality rates in the world.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At the beginning, it was because we had such tight restrictions, rapid contact tracing and low total number of cases in the community.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But with cases rising fast, the case fatality rate remains low now because we have reached such a high vaccination rate and because all those who have become sick have been able to receive the care that they need.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our healthcare system is stressed, but it has not been overwhelmed, unlike many countries last year, where patients had to be turned away and doctors had to choose amongst many patients whom to save.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These other countries experienced what is known as excess mortality, as the pandemic spread rapidly through the population and hospitals were overwhelmed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Excess mortality is when a lot more people die in a year than you expect.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are trying very hard to avoid that, by keeping restrictions tight last year when our population was vulnerable to the disease and then cautiously opening up after we vaccinated the vast majority of our population.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Even then, we have to accept there will be some deaths.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our goal is to make sure that there are no significant excess deaths, as a result of an inability to provide adequate medical care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so far, that is something that we have been able to do and that we want to keep doing.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Up until recently we kept the absolute number of deaths small by ensuring that few people caught COVID-19 and also that those who were infected got good treatment and care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Now that we have to live with COVID-19, we will continue to protect people from getting infected through vaccination and safe management measures, but this protection is not complete.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And that is why much larger numbers will get infected.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But we will continue to make sure that those who are infected get good treatment and care, and so keep the death rate from COVID-19 as low as possible.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Hence, we are doing everything we can to expand our ICU capacity and protect our healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our death rate is 0.2%, compared to 3% or more in countries that experienced a surge in cases before vaccination.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This rate of 0.2% is comparable to catching pneumonia – pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Most of these will be the elderly and those who are already unwell.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These are also mostly the elderly and the unwell.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That is why we keep emphasising the importance of vaccination and boosters.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have managed to continue to provide excellent healthcare for all COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 patients.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I am extremely proud of my colleagues, co-workers and friends who man the wards, clinics, and many other sites where they perform their duties and we should place a high value on maintaining the standard.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And we are trying to get there without excess mortality.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But no other country has done that before.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Nearly every other country that has arrived at that destination has paid a high price in lives.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I hope my explanation has helped Members understand why although we say we are living with COVID-19, we cannot just open up and risk having the number of cases shoot up, because more and more cases will translate into more and more ICU beds used.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Beyond a certain point, that will force us to accept a lower standard of care, and hence, have more deaths that could have been prevented.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Despite our best efforts, events may overtake us and we may have no choice in the matter.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If, despite our caution, ICU cases rise sharply, we will still do our very best to look after every patient.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would strongly prefer if we can avoid that dreadful scenario.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We need to continue to manage the overall number of cases in our population, even as we continue to increase our hospital capacity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The main reason why we got to this point in the fight with COVID-19 with such low mortality rates is our people.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I have spoken at length about the staff that I met at the ICUs and this applies to all our healthcare workers in the emergency departments, the clinics, the PHPCs, our swabbers, our contact tracers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Across every sector, everyone has given their all, together with an ongoing commitment to excellence in service.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: MOH and the healthcare teams will continue to train staff, increase beds and expand ICU capacity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: My MOH colleagues and I will keep working directly with the ICU directors and clinical leads to help them.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They know better than me how to manage the patients, to provide clinical care, but they need support, resources and policies that allow them to optimise their outcomes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will help to look after them and their staff.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: All of us can continue to play our part.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Vaccination remains critical, every single extra person who gets vaccinated makes a difference, to themselves and for all of us.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Getting your booster shot as soon as you are eligible makes a difference.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Following the safe management measures makes a difference.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Using the right healthcare resources appropriately makes a difference.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Eventually, enough of us will be vaccinated or will have been infected, that we will see the case numbers come down and the situation stabilise.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It happened because Singaporeans stood together, looked out for each other, did their duty and put the interests of others ahead of their own.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And the healthcare workers of Singapore have done all this and much, much, more, caring for us all.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I received another message from a colleague: "we are one of the few countries in the world where ICU teams don't have to worry about resources and equipment – very grateful for that.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Healthcare workers have given everything in the last two years, we have held ourselves up to the highest standards; we have the lowest mortality in the world; our people are still pushing on".

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The healthcare workers we are worried about are also the same healthcare workers who are committed to doing what is needed to look after all their patients.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They will do their duty, do their best and try their hardest.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Words will never be enough, but I express our gratitude on behalf of this House.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given that seniors, especially those who are not vaccinated, are most susceptible to severe illnesses due to COVID-19, can there be initiatives to identify, isolate and protect these seniors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And thus, if we can implement such measures to protect seniors in an effective way, is the Ministry prepared to consider loosening safe management measures for the rest of the population?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In a way, that is what we are trying to do with our vaccination-differentiated measures: expose some people to a lower level of risk while allowing other parts of our population to do the things that make life a bit more bearable.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But there is only so far that we can go.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you are a senior and you are unwell and, for some reason, unvaccinated, you cannot be isolated completely.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You need fresh air, food, contact with other people.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I understand what the Member is asking.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But there is another dimension to this question.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Because it supposes that the seniors and the vulnerable are a different segment of the population from the rest of us, who are younger, healthier and vaccinated.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The truth is, we interact and we meet and we pass infections on to them.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think the experience of the last two years, in a way, has demonstrated just how much intermingling and interconnectedness there is between all kinds of networks and communities here in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We want to go and look after our parents.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Each of those interactions poses a very small but measurable risk to them as well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I think we have to assume that whatever it is that we are doing, we must treat the whole population as one.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will try with the vaccination-differentiated measures but there is only so far that we can go.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The first supplementary question is about whether we can make vaccination mandatory since the vaccine now has been fully approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I filed a Parliamentary Question asking when will HSA make the vaccine not used under emergency use, which means it can be fully licensed to use for normal times.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You can imagine that for something like childhood vaccines, you may say that without it, you cannot have access to play groups or school.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is a specific thing that you want to do and for that, you are getting the vaccine.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But here, we are talking about all the normal activities of life and so policing it, executing it, implementing it is not without challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many people contributed to this fight against COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have the people who do all the swabs, supervise our self-swabs, the people who run our vaccination centres, people who make sure the vaccines arrive on Singapore shores, the people who do conveyancing every day – hundreds, thousands of trips to and fro, hospitals to treatment facilities – all our officers on the ground, safe distancing ambassadors, our vendors who disinfect places that we have been to, teachers who kept schools going for past 20 months, preschool teachers included, social workers, our community volunteers who help out those who are in need.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We all owe a debt of gratitude to all of them for collectively putting up this fight.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But as Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary has very vividly and, in a very heartfelt way, described, I think the role of healthcare workers is especially important.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are not like the other frontliners, they are also our last line of defence.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, while the rest of Singapore try to get back to a normal life, we try to get back to work, to travel for work or study, they bear that disproportionate responsibility.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If something goes wrong, they are the ones who carry the burden and are literally the last line of defence, while the rest of us can continue our work and life.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think what the numbers suggest, and what the numbers we have now insofar as ICU capacity is concerned, is that there is yet sufficient potential for upscaling the number of ICU beds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of course, the assumption being that this remark that was made on 13 August refers both to the bed itself, the ancillary equipment needed and the manpower needed to manage 1,000 beds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is this still the operating parameter or have things changed quite significantly?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second point is somewhat connected but it is with regard to the measures introduced vis-a-vis the Stabilisation Phase.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think there has been some pushback in terms of retaining the number of two individuals in a dining capacity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is significant public feedback that this should be increased to five, especially for vaccinated individuals, particularly since the Government is also opening up more Vaccinated Travel Lanes (VTLs) and lifting travel bans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At least, for the South Asian group of countries, this was lifted very recently.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, there is a view that cannot quite connect why dining capacity cannot be opened up in view of the number of vaccinated individuals who actually are not imposing on the ICU capacity as much as non-vaccinated individuals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I hope there could be some clarity provided insofar as what is holding the Government back on this number, on opening up at least for dining for up to five individuals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Senior Minister of State said in his Statement that the recruitment of healthcare workers from overseas is continuing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, it will be helpful to have the numbers that are coming on board as well and not just the numbers that are leaving.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will take the first two questions and maybe Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary can also comment on the first question and answer the third.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I remember quite vividly that we talked about the possibility of ramping up to 1,000 beds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I spoke about it at a press conference illustrating how if cases doubled every week, in five weeks, the beds will actually be exhausted.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is the illustration that even with that kind of capacity, if infections run away from us, it will be of no use.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We would just get overwhelmed in a matter of weeks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I also remember vividly – do not even get near that – not even near the 1,000 limit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary is a lot more experienced in this and he knows it inside out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think he had explained that we have all the logistics and all the consumables to set it up but I think manpower will be a serious constraint.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think not without a major degradation of care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think it is not a black-and-white kind of situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With every step up in the number of beds, there is degradation of care and there is a trade-off.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second question on whether we can increase dining to five for vaccinated diners.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We were even at eight at one point.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because when you meet with five, as explained by Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary, you do increase the risk of transmission.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If it is transmission within vaccinated individuals, it may not be that serious.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we also live with older people, with seniors who may be unvaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And we can inadvertently bring the virus to them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have a neighbour, an unvaccinated senior and she has streams of visitors coming to visit her, persuading her to get vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I was persuading their visitors maybe stop coming to persuade her, just give her a call.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we do have to pay attention to that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is always a comparison with why is it that we can open for travel but not for dine-in.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The difference is this, that in the initial stage, Singapore has very low infections and the world around us has very high infection rates.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, when you open up borders at that time, you are opening up the floodgates.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our infection rates and the rates outside are similar.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, they may have lower infections than us because they went through huge waves and we are still going through ours.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Furthermore, we limit travel or SHN-free travel to only vaccinated individuals and at the border, you are subject to tests.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, theoretically, if you can have an event, like a wedding, a bigger wedding, everybody is subject to a test, you can sit in fives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This also present possibilities for the MTF to think about in future, whether through testing, through vaccination, we can allow gathering that is a bit less restrictive.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are all possibilities that we will continue to think about.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But I think one of the challenges we have to appreciate is that even if we recruit from overseas, anybody coming into that environment is new, they are inexperienced.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: By definition, they are inexperienced with the environment, our healthcare protocols, but they may actually be literally new in terms of their training as well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, their role is going to be quite different.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It will make a difference in other parts of our ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If I may make a comment on the first part that Minister for Health talked about, some of the uncertainties are about how long we have to carry a certain load or a certain number of patients within the ICU.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you have a terrible disaster, mass casualty, a very bad accident, you may have many times the number of patients that we currently have in the ICU.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But as a one-off incident, the patients will not stay as long.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What we have today is the equivalent of a low-intensity conflict and having to be on readiness and high alert for weeks and weeks, and months and months.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Your surge capacity at the start of a low-intensity conflict is very, very different after two years or after one month.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Even this current surge when it started, there was really no way to know or model how long it was going to last and what the peak of peaks would be.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, what the Minister talked about is the logistical planning parameter.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you do not have 1,000 bed spaces, you know that you cannot get there.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But if you do, that is physically where you can locate people.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The manpower issue is not something that we can do a simple calculation for.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As I said, it depends on how long this goes on for, how long the peak goes on for.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Crucially, today, coming to the end of 2021, the amount that we can reduce business-as-usual is really quite different from where we were, let us say, six months ago; in fact, where we were, even three months ago.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That is an additional factor that we have to take into account.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State explain why has the number of deaths increased by such a large number?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is it due to the relaxation of rules?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is there anything else we can do to cut down on the number of deaths because every life lost is a tragedy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The first is that the base number of our population that is being infected with COVID-19 has risen very, very significantly compared to the time period that he was talking about.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The second is that although some patients with COVID-19 who pass on, will pass on very soon after getting the infection, most will take a long time to get seriously ill and may take some time before they succumb, which is a testament to the care that we have put in place and their attempts to fight the infection.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are people who are infected, perhaps, two weeks ago, maybe even a month ago.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: After you get the infection, it takes time before you develop the need to go on oxygen support.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And then, once you are on oxygen, not everybody will go on to the ICU or succumb, but it takes time for conditions to worsen to the point where then you need further care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, there are two main reasons why the deaths are rising in total number: baseline has increased and it is that effect of the lag.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But I stress, the proportion of patients who then succumb has not changed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Well, vaccinations, as I have explained; booster jabs, as I have explained.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But even if you have had those, you may have other underlying illnesses and the underlying illnesses need to be well-controlled.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, if you have diabetes, control your diabetes well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you are requiring medication, take your medication regularly, comply with all the usual prescriptions around maintaining good health.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For those of us that are fortunate not to have health problems, all the usual rules apply: eat better, sleep better, get more exercise and reach out to your loved ones.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And if you are a smoker, stop smoking.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you get a lung infection with COVID-19 and you have knocked out some of your lung function through smoking, you are not off to a good start.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These are the ways in which we can prevent mortality and morbidity in COVID-19.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Like him, I am very much grateful for the efforts that our healthcare workers and frontline workers have put in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is half that of the OECD average.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And only Japan, among those that have lower ICU beds per 100,000 of the population has a significantly larger elderly share of the population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, the question here is: if we know, as we did in the earlier half of this year, that we were going into an endemic surge, why is it that during this lull period, there was not a more concerted effort in increasing our capacity and this, of course, includes bringing in relevant manpower, as Senior Minister of State Janil mentioned was the big challenge?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second question builds on this issue of manpower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My question is whether looking forward, Singapore would be competitive in attracting these foreign nurses, and if not, what steps are being made to expand our local nursing and doctor workforce to ensure that we are able to meet our future needs?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, it is not that we did not have spare capacity pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But as I have already also explained, if you wanted to open up more of this capacity and keep it empty, it would have an impact on resources that could have been applied elsewhere.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I do not know if that addresses his first question about why we did not do more before we knew about COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think comparing with other countries is fraught in this situation because the number does not reflect, for example, clinical practices, the demographics in terms of the health patterns that they have.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I do not think one can take the view that there is a certain number of ICU beds that you must have per population.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some of these also rest on what counts as an ICU admission.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is quite different from country to country because of the way in which the nurses are licensed, the way in which drugs are licensed, the way in which doctors practise.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: He then asked about a more concerted effort to increase capacity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Well, it is not that we stood still and waited to see what happened.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the thing about ICU manpower, you cannot stand it up and have it lying around waiting.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If a year ago, we said we needed to increase our manpower by three times or by four times, what would those nurses have been doing in the ensuing 12 months or six months?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They certainly would not have been getting experience at ICU care because you need to look after ICU patients in order to become an ICU-trained staff.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, you can see that what we have been doing is opening up capacity ahead of the curve, but not so far ahead of the curve that we are having people sit around idle, while other services are undermanned or unmanned.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But ahead of the curve, so that we can do some of that training and redeployment training and redeployment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Intensive care, critical care, whether you talk about the doctors, the nurses, the respiratory therapists, the social workers, the pharmacists that are deployed in there, it is a clinical practice.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is not something that you can learn and be ready for by reading textbooks and doing online courses.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You have to be mentored and precepted into looking after patients with your hands, eyes and senses.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, it is not something that you could have gone five X, four X, in vacuo in peacetime and held everything ready in abeyance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And I say this not as matter of hyperbole but that lowest mortality rate in the world is matched by any number of other patient care and clinical quality indicators which I think we and our healthcare workers should be justifiably proud of.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I think, my supplementary question really is, despite this increase, how do I benchmark 80%?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Is it something that we are still being too conservative about and part of the increase to 350 ICU beds will still be able to come from this pool?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Or is it really something we should be really quite concerned about, because if my Math serves me right, 63% occupancy of 298 beds in 2019 means a 188 non-COVID-19 ICU beds being occupied versus 130 today that you are saying 80% of 163?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Are we just putting less people in ICU today?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And is there really no impact or no deterioration on patient outcomes?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Maybe I can start with the last part first, which is, is there no impact and no deterioration?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And I think the statements and quotes from my professional colleagues, what I have described as the conditions under which they are working and their concerns for themselves, that is the impact.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But there has not been a deterioration, that is the outcomes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, it is through their heroic efforts, their resolve, their resilience and, frankly, the excellence of the people that we have in our healthcare system, that in these conditions, as a result of this impact on our manpower deployment, they have been able to deliver excellent clinical outcomes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think the uncertainty is how long do we expect them to do this for?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think in this issue of being too conservative or do we have the right number of beds, maybe I can try to phrase it the other way around.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: First, let me assume that she agrees with me that actually we cannot over-divert resources from non-COVID-19 patients to stand by for COVID-19 patients that have not arrived yet.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: People will have heart attacks, people will have accidents and they will need care; and if you have nurses, doctors, beds ready only to accept COVID-19 patients and not to accept all these other conditions, we will see an increased death rate, we will see excess mortality not from COVID-19, but from all these other conditions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, we must increase slowly step by step trying to be just ahead of the curve.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ultimately, as I say, we may end up having to accept a lower standard of care, but we will want the lower standard of care, as it were, to be evenly spread across so that no part of the system breaks, that everybody is under some degree of strain and going through this together.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But in terms of maybe understanding where we are, the 63% of certain number of beds, 280 beds, it is a bit hard to grasp in terms of the proportions because we keep changing the denominator.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We keep increasing the number of ICU beds.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will come to that in a minute.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But if you look at the actual number of patients that we have in the ICU, the actual number of patients that our care teams are working on, it is about between 130 and 140 non-COVID-19 ICU patients, what we would call the business-as-usual patients; and today, it is about 130, a few days ago is 139 for COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, let us say about 135 each, about half-half, that is 270 ICU patients across the hospital ecosystem that our teams have to manage.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, that is a workload increase to 150%.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You can sustain that for a short period of time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Can you sustain that for a prolonged period of time?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I hope that answers the Member's questions in terms of are we being conservative or are we planning ahead.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What we are hoping to do is chart a middle path, ramp up capacity just ahead of demand, with enough time to give the staff some degree of orientation, training and be ready for when the surge comes in, but not so much that we end up sacrificing the rest of our healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That would be the inappropriate thing to do.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are trying to tread a middle ground.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I join the Minister and Senior Minister of State in expressing my deepest gratitude to our healthcare workers for fighting this battle on the frontlines and holding the fort in very trying conditions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, based on the situation that Senior Minister of State outlined, it appears the number of healthcare workers is the limiting factor for further reopening.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Since healthcare human resource capacity cannot be easily ramped up and our vaccination coverage is almost maximised, what prospect then is there for a further reopening anytime soon?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Others can register their interest but are not guaranteed the booking.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, in the interest of maximising vaccine coverage and minimising hospitalisations, can MOH make Sinovac generally available to all those who have not been vaccinated but simply prefer to get that vaccine, whatever the merits of that preference are?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The availability of healthcare workers is not what will decide whether we reopen or do not reopen.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is how many with severe illnesses and how many deaths we are prepared to tolerate in that controlled process of getting to the point whereas a combination of vaccination, boosters and mild or asymptomatic infections, our overall population is much, much more resistant to COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Getting there is not a function of how many healthcare workers we have.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: How many deaths we have on the road to that destination is a function of how many healthcare workers we have and how many cases we can manage at a time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, as I have said and as many other people have said, this will pass, this will get better.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do not know exactly when but we are building up our entire society's immunity and resilience against COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And as we do so, every day that passes, every extra time that we can hold the situation, we are more likely to be able to open up safely.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: When we do lighten restrictions, you can expect there will be more cases and there will be more waves.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But if our immunity and our resilience is built up, each wave will be less threatening, there will be less cases than the last.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And hence, our restrictions do not have to be anywhere near as tight.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I do not know that I have answered his question directly, but I disagree with the way he has framed it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And I hope he understands the explanation that I have given.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And what we are concerned about is what happens if you get the infection despite having had the vaccination.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Sinovac is available as an option when that is not possible.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, it is better than nothing, but it is not what we would see as the most appropriate, given that it is the Delta variant that is spreading through our population and given that we are trying to avoid serious illnesses and convert this infection into a mild infection.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I also want to join the rest of the Members here to salute the efforts put in by the healthcare workers for doing such a wonderful job so far.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, I would like to raise the issue of ICU beds from the other perspective.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We note that one of the most important indicators as the Senior Minister of State and Minister have said that MOH is watching, is the utilisation rate of the ICU beds.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to clarify the following: if the utilisation of the ICU beds is acceptable, that is, not overly stretched and even the daily cases are about two, three thousand a day, does it mean that we are prepared to live with this high number for the next one, two months?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If so, are we prepared to remove some of the restrictions or lessen some the restrictions of COVID-19?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng is correct that the high total number, because 99% are asymptomatic, does not in itself mean whether we can lift or not lift restrictions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What we have to look at is the number of cases that require assistance and help from our healthcare system and make sure that we are able to provide for that.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But it is not the case that only looking at the ICU utilisation rate will we then make the decision.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The reason is we have a much larger group of people who require oxygen.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Because as the total number of patients increases, the total number of patients requiring oxygen will also increase in proportion.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, he is right but there is a little bit more nuance to the consideration.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, this is why in the previous MTF press conference, they talked about the doubling rate or the expansion rate of the ICU care.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is whether we think it is going up and how fast we think it is going up or coming back down here.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, these are some of the factors we have to take into account, Sir.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the various routes of infection, especially for the seniors?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because that is the base where the subsequent fatality comes about, which the Senior Minister of State has shared just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, there are some rumours, unconfirmed information in the public arena, that a lot of these seniors, those who are living alone, come from the nursing homes and those who are infected in their own homes, together with their children — how many of them are actually having another COVID-19 patient inside the home, under the Home Recovery Programme?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, these various routes of infection would be something that, I think, we hope to get more information from the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second is that, while we are saying that the fatality had gone up, are there changes in our treatment protocols for the seniors in the hospital?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And then, is there a possibility that we have some preventive treatments for seniors and also for other citizens or other residents in our country, to lower the risk of COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, in other words, are there potential treatments that we can introduce?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So far, there has not been a lot of information on that from the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And thirdly, of course, the most sensitive topic right now in our society is that: is there a justification to impose vaccination differentiation on the whole group of unvaccinated people?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, maybe there is very little leeway that we can actually convince them to get vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are healthy and so, is it appropriate to also impose the vaccination differentiation policy on them, especially the latest MOM advisory which actually may affect their livelihood?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it fair to impose something that destroys a livelihood of a person who chooses not to be vaccinated?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would point out that his questions have some contradictions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: He asked if there was a change or some treatment which could prevent COVID-19 for seniors who either get sick or get unwell.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I presume that by asking that question, he then requires us to use a preventive treatment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If I propose to him that there is a preventive treatment which is 10 times effective, it would reduce your risk by 10 times, he may even then ask me to mandate it and require it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are trying to prevent them from becoming sick and overwhelming our healthcare system so that them and the rest of us, then do not lose the ability to have good care for heart disease, diabetes and cancer, and all the other things we need healthcare for.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, his second and third questions seem to me to contradict each other and I think he needs to decide does he believe that we should be fairly liberal about this and choose to allow people to take on for themselves a really unacceptable degree of risk and impose the consequences of that risk on all of us?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Or does he want us to go and tell people exactly what to do and constrain their lives in a way that protects all of us?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: He seems to, in his two questions, choose extremes at one end of the other.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are trying to tread a middle path and trying to get the best of both.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: He asks then what caused the infections in our country and what are the routes of infection for seniors who are living alone, in their own homes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you were truly isolated and you were entirely living alone, with no human contact, you could maybe get away without this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But I think, people find that sort of life is also fairly unbearable.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, whether you are living alone as a senior or in a nursing home or in your own home, usually there is some form of human contact.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And that is precisely why we cannot think of our population as the seniors and the rest of us, the unvaccinated and the rest of us.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We intermingle and we meet each other and we pass on the infection to each other.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our vaccine-differentiated measures are trying to make the risk lower for one than the other, but it is not about separating us out into completely separate populations and that would not be possible.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I know that you have said that patients with underlying conditions, even if well-controlled, will still be at a higher risk of death; and that not being vaccinated will put Singaporeans at an even higher risk.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Could I ask if currently MOH has any data on the percentage of vaccinated patients who have died from COVID-19 who have underlying conditions that are actually well-controlled; and if not, would MOH consider tracking this?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Because the definition of well-controlled will vary and the way in which you see the impact of good control of the disease when you get COVID-19 will also be quite different.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you have had diabetes for many years, diagnosed young, struggling with it, living with it, but you have had it kind of controlled.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Do you have a lower risk than someone who perhaps had it diagnosed only one or two years ago, but really has not had it well-controlled yet?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I am not entirely sure what the answer to that question is.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And when you then encounter COVID-19, even if you had it well-controlled, because your body is fighting another illness, now COVID-19, your diabetes control goes out.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, do you then look at well-controlled at the point that you got infected, or the point that you got into ICU?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The data that we have does not help to inform us to the point where we can make a recommendation and we can say, "Well, if you have diabetes and your blood sugar is like this, you are okay; if your blood sugar is like that, it is not okay".

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are still at the point where we say, "If you have diabetes, control it as best you can.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Whether you have COVID-19 or not, that is a risk.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Now that COVID-19 is present, you need to really make sure you take care of yourself." And this then applies to a wide variety of conditions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, it is quite clear that poorly controlled diseases do increase the risk very significantly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But there are some patients even with well-controlled diseases, it appears that having that disease means that they handle COVID-19 poorly even if the disease was well-controlled when they get COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I hope that adds some clarity to the Member's question.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Part of that is because we do operate as one system and where there is a little bit of capacity here or there, there is some load balancing and different sites work together.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, that is going to be dynamic, they are working to try to clear this as best they can.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And probably, you may have some people who are on leave but have a relatively short notice to be present, or they may be on local leave and another proportion which are allowed overseas leave and so forth.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think these are operational parameters and you have to let the clinical teams make these decisions on their own.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We need to try to support them at a more systemic level.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I want to make a comment but also to go back to two questions that were raised earlier.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One is by the Member, Mr Gerald Giam, who asked about Sinovac.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Yesterday, I think a few hundreds did so, covered by Zaobao.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you are below 60, you have to make an appointment, but it is generally available.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second point I want to mention is what Mr Leong Mun Wai raised, where he talked about some rumours.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am not sure you can repeat rumours in this House; I will leave it to the Leader.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But he mentioned something about "nursing home", something about "home transmission".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The large majority is actually transmission within the community.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But out of that 10%, 8% get it very early on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That means at the point of entry into quarantine or into Health Risk Warning (HRW), you are tested and you are positive; suggesting that actually, they got it at the same time as the index case.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, during the subsequent days, another 2% then got transmitted.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, I think from the evidence that we have been tracking so far, the incidence of transmitting at home, so long as you take the precautions, is actually not high.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The high transmissions still happen within the community, through person-to-person interaction.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I want to just maybe make some general comments after hearing all the questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Dealing with COVID-19 is quite different from business or organisation planning, where you know that this season or this month, if it is coming to Christmas, business is going to go up, so, let us plan for it, make sure we have manpower and capacity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we are looking at a crisis of a generation, a global pandemic crisis, not something that we plan year-to-year based on seasons or a five-year plan.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It hits you and it overwhelms the healthcare system all over the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You look at the papers today on the G20 meeting and in France and Italy, life seems to be normal, but we forget what they went through last year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Go back, dig up the papers last year on how the whole healthcare system was overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Regardless of what you say about their ICU provisions and all that, or their healthcare workers' provisions, when COVID-19 hit those societies, they were totally overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Doctors had to choose who got the hospital bed, who did not, who they had to save and who does not get saved.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Those were the painful human tragedies that happened and the big human price that they paid to get to where they are today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked, how do we prevent and minimise death?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We prevent and minimise death by making sure we do not go through that, of what other countries have gone through.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Whether it is the US, the UK, France, Germany, Italy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We avoid excess death by avoiding that, by preventing that totally.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One says zero-COVID-19 strategy is the right way to go.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One says, no, you have to have living-with-COVID-19 strategies and maybe even Freedom Day.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Last year, before we had vaccinations, when we were vulnerable to the disease, we took a zero-COVID-19 strategy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, we went on to a national vaccination programme, got ourselves to about 70% to 75% by National Day.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, we said, zero-COVID-19 is over, we need to start opening up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But yet, we do not take another dogmatic approach to say we must go for Freedom Day and open up all at once.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we take the middle path: not total lockdown, neither is it Freedom Day, but we open up gradually.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Making sure that it can cope, given the infection rate and how that translates into ICU cases and to people who fall severely ill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary said, with each passing day, with more vaccinations and some people recovered well and built up natural immunity, we accumulated antibodies and resilience within our society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I know Members of this House, including myself, all wish that life goes back to normal, that we can have dining in five or more, we can have our proper wedding dinners and events, go back to our grassroots functions and community functions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We all wish we can all do that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do not have to sit up there in the Gallery anymore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Everybody can sit in the Chamber, engaging each other.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We all wish to do that and I think we will get there.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We get there by continuing this path, building up our antibodies day by day.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do not know how long it would take.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Prime Minister said maybe three months, maybe six.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We wish it is shorter rather than longer.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But many countries have gone through the process and reached there, and we shall reach there too.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have a Personal Explanation from Ms Raeesah Khan.
